full_judgment:
25. Without multiplying the instances in which, if no interim order can be passed, the ultimate order that may be passed would become totally ineffective, it would not be contrary to the intention of Parliament to say that no absolute prohibition has been imposed on the Court's power to do justice by the amended clause (2) of Article 102. We do not, however, in saying so import some limitations which Parliament did not intend but we only find some limitations which impliedly qualify the prohibition which is not city express but may other wise seem absolute. To reconcile tilts expression sneeringly imposing on unrestraint  prohibition with the need to do justice, what is imperative to consider in this regard is the need for judicial self restraint. While it is necessary that the Constitutional command in clause (2) of article 102 must be obeyed by this Court, it is also no less necessary that what the Constitution has commanded it to do by clause (1) must also equally be obeyed by the Court. If the two commands may at times seem conflicting with each other, it must not prove to be so battling as to defeat the judicial skill or ingenuity. If the making of an order would seem not only urgent but unless it be made the final order would become infructuous one of the two alternatives may be considered Sufficient to end the judicial dileimma, namely, (1) the Court can instantly hear the inatter after a very short interval enabling the service of notice on the respondents and pass the final order, or (2) the Court may, after hearing the respondents, make the necessary order, or it could even pass an order to maintain the status quo between the parties to the controversy if it becomes apparent that the final order would be  vain and ineffective. If there be any case which is not covered by any of these alternatives, it would really be an extreme case which at present we are unable to foresee and, therefore, suggest any solution. 

 "In my judgment, the change of language can properly be regarded as indicating an intention to make some, alteration, but the question remains ; What was the  alteration which was intended? In deciding that well-settled principles requires us to go to the words of the new Act. We can have in mind the circumstances when the Act was passed and the mischief which then exited so far as these are common knowledge, but we can only use these matters as an aid to the construction of the words which Parliament has used. We cannot encroach on its legislative function by reading in some limitation within we may think was properly intended but which cannot be inferred from the words of the Act."
